subjective.question: Define assessment. (2 marks) Assessment is the process of gathering and discussing information from multiple and diverse sources in order to develop a deep understanding of what students know, understand, and can do with their knowledge as a result of their educational experiences. The process culminates when assessment results are used to improve subsequent learning.

How will you teach the topic "Matter" to young students? Demonstrate. (2 marks) Matter is taught through hands-on exploration rather than definitions. The teacher gives children a wooden block (solid), water in a transparent glass (liquid) and balloons (gas). Children observe that a solid has a distinct shape which does not change in different containers, a liquid has no shape of its own and takes the shape of its container and can be poured, and a gas cannot be seen but can be felt, as in a blown balloon. Children then identify solids, liquids and gases in their surroundings and record their properties in charts, so the concept of matter is built from their own observations.

What is the purpose of the science subject? (2 marks) Science is taught to nurture future scientists, technologists and engineers; to increase the number of scientifically literate adults in society and improve the public understanding of science; and to equip students with skills that are useful across disciplines, such as evidence-based reasoning, critical thinking, problem solving and specialized ways of social interaction. The goal of K-8 science education is to develop a strong base of scientific knowledge and practices that enables students to engage in deeper understanding of science in higher grades.

How is a hypothesis formed in the scientific approach? (3 marks) In the scientific approach, a hypothesis is formed after careful observation of an object, event or phenomenon and raising questions about it. The learner then proposes a tentative explanation for the phenomenon which is consistent with the evidence collected and with ideas from prior experiences. This tentative explanation is the hypothesis; predictions are made from it and an investigation is planned and carried out to test whether the hypothesis is supported by the data or not.

Explain the term predicting. (3 marks) Predicting is forecasting the outcome of a specific future event based on a pattern of evidence or on a hypothesis (an explanation). When predicting, learners make use of evidence from experience or of a possible explanation in forecasting outcomes of specific events that go beyond the data. A prediction is not a wild guess; its sub-skills include justifying a prediction in terms of a pattern in the evidence and making a prediction in order to test a hypothesis.

How does mercury rise in a thermometer? Explain the concept of the effect of heat on gases and water to students. (5 marks) Liquids and gases expand when they are heated, and this property is used in a liquid-in-glass thermometer: as the temperature rises, the mercury (or alcohol) in the bulb expands and rises up the narrow tube, and the height of the column shows the temperature. This is demonstrated to students in two ways. First, an empty plastic bottle with a balloon fixed on its mouth is placed in hot water; the air inside expands with heat and the balloon starts inflating, showing that gases expand on heating. Second, a bottle one-third filled with colored water, with a straw sealed in its top, is placed in hot water; the colored water rises in the straw, showing that liquids also expand on heating. Students conclude that fluids expand with heating, which is exactly how a thermometer works.

Write the complete procedure of lesson planning and its steps of execution. (5 marks) A lesson plan is prepared and executed through the following components: 1) Overview of the lesson. 2) Learning objectives, divided into three categories: (a) concepts, (b) skills/practices, (c) attitudes. 3) Background: the teacher evaluates himself/herself and improves his/her own knowledge of the content before entering the classroom. 4) Children's ideas: the topic is discussed with children to explore their prior ideas, and concepts are taught at the students' level of learning. 5) Materials: easily available and cheap material is arranged for each child, for each group and for the entire class. 6) Preparation of the material and charts before the lesson. 7) Procedure/Methodology: the step-by-step classroom activity through which children observe, investigate, record and discuss. 8) Homework. 9) Assessment of children's learning against the objectives.

What is Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK)? Explain its components. Pedagogical Content Knowledge is the knowledge a teacher needs to teach a subject effectively. It includes: (1) an in-depth understanding of the content of the discipline being taught, i.e. the ideas, concepts, skills and practices associated with that discipline; (2) an understanding of how students learn that subject, what is hard and what is easy for them, and what examples, processes and activities will help them learn, i.e. appropriate pedagogy adapted to the different development levels and interests of the learners; (3) knowledge of how children's understanding of core ideas builds across K-8; (4) knowledge of the conceptual ideas students hold in the earliest grades and their ideas about science itself; and (5) the ability to assess children's developing ideas over time and to interpret and respond instructionally to the results of assessment.

Describe the nature of scientific knowledge. What is a scientific theory? Science constitutes an organized body of knowledge about the natural world and the processes/practices whereby this body of knowledge is established and is continuously being extended, refined and revised. A scientific theory is an explanation of observed phenomena and natural objects which can command widespread acceptance and significant testing. Through testing and refinement it becomes a well-established description of phenomena in a particular area and provides a coherent conceptual framework consistent with the body of facts currently known. A theory is valued if it can make testable, precise predictions for as yet unmeasured or unobserved effects. Scientific knowledge is modified or altered in the light of accurate and reliable data/evidence, and scientists must identify and avoid uncertainties and bias associated with the investigator, instruments and methods.

Explain the seven process skills of science. The seven process skills are: 1) Observing: using the senses and extending the senses by using tools or instruments as necessary to gather information about an object, event or phenomenon. 2) Questioning: raising questions about an object, event or phenomenon, including recognizing and asking investigable questions. 3) Hypothesizing: attempting to give explanations which are consistent with evidence or with ideas from prior experiences. 4) Predicting: forecasting the outcome of a specific future event based on a pattern of evidence or a hypothesis. 5) Planning and investigating: designing an investigation that includes procedures to collect reliable data, including identifying and controlling variables for a fair test. 6) Interpreting and analyzing data: considering evidence, evaluating and drawing conclusions by assessing the data, and identifying patterns or trends in observations or measurements. 7) Communicating: representing observations, ideas, models or conclusions by talking, writing, drawing, making physical models, tables, graphs and charts. In actual practice these skills are not individual skills but combinations or blends of several skills, and students use them to build a conceptual understanding of science content.

What is prior knowledge? Why is it important in science teaching? Prior knowledge is the knowledge and ideas learners already have before new teaching begins. It affects how the learner perceives new information and how a student organizes new information; learners construct concepts from prior knowledge, assimilating new information into their existing schema. Children develop ideas, based on their everyday experiences, about natural phenomena before they are taught science in school. Some of these ideas agree with scientific views and can act as resources for learning, but some intuitive understandings contradict scientific explanations and pose obstacles to science learning. Therefore teachers need to be aware of children's prior or existing ideas, of the learning goals, and of the difference between the two when planning and teaching, so that they can take appropriate steps to bridge the gap. Instruction must be based on what children already know.

What is conceptual change? How can teachers help bring it about? Conceptual change is a process of transition from ordinary ways of perceiving, directing attention, conceptualizing, reasoning and justifying; slowly, learners transform prior knowledge to accommodate new scientific ideas. Some concepts are relatively easy because they are consistent with students' initial understanding, while others are difficult because they call for fundamental revisions to children's initial structure. Traditional instruction and simple discovery learning alone have failed to bring about such change. Teachers can facilitate it by: teaching concepts in the context of an organizing theme or bigger picture; investigating and gathering data that expose students to discrepant events and sharing ideas to resolve the discrepancy; and providing lots of opportunities to strengthen understanding of new ideas through extended application and collective reflection, since a reflective component makes it possible to learn things that might never be figured out through trial and error.

Differentiate between the traditional approach and the inquiry-based approach to teaching science. 1) In the traditional approach, content is taught before doing any activity, hence activities confirm the content; in inquiry-based curricula, activity leads to the content or to the discovery of content. 2) In the traditional approach, information is given to students when they are taught content, whereas the inquiry approach focuses on building the concepts of students. 3) In the traditional classroom, students have no role in planning the lesson or activity; in the inquiry classroom, students are involved in the lessons. 4) The traditional approach is teacher directed, while in the inquiry approach students are involved in activities and directions are given by the teacher. 5) The focus of the traditional approach is on obtaining the right answers, while the inquiry approach focuses on the process of learning that students undergo during the investigative process. Inquiry itself has stages: structured inquiry (questions and procedure are given, students collect data), guided inquiry (questions are given, students plan the investigation) and open inquiry (students generate their own questions and plan the investigation).

Compare formative and summative assessment, giving examples of each. Formative assessment provides feedback and information during the instructional process, while learning is taking place; it measures student progress and is used to decide the next steps in teaching. Its examples include observations during in-class activities, homework exercises, reflection journals, question and answer sessions, conferences between instructor and student, and in-class activities where students informally present their results. Summative assessment takes place after the learning has been completed and provides information and feedback that sums up the teaching and learning process; all students are evaluated according to common criteria so results can be compared, and the information is used to report what has been learnt, determine grades and make decisions about promotion. Its examples include major examinations, the final examination, performances, student evaluation of the course and instructor self-evaluation. Inquiry-based teaching provides continuous opportunities for formative assessment.

What is a fair test? Describe the fair test template. An investigation is fair, that is, its results are reliable, provided only one quantity is changed and the rest are held constant. For example, jelly crystals dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water can only be concluded fairly if the amount of jelly powder and the amount of water are kept the same in both cups and only the temperature of the water is changed. The fair test template has four main features: 1) What is our experiment / what are we investigating? 2) What are we changing? 3) What are we keeping the same? 4) What do we find out?

Describe the properties of solids, liquids and gases. Solids have a distinct shape which does not change when they are placed in different containers; solids are dry and many solids are hard, i.e. their shape does not change easily when pressed. Liquids have no distinct shape of their own but take the shape of the container they are in; liquids flow and can be poured; liquids are wet. Gases, like liquids, do not have a shape of their own and take the shape of the container they are in; they usually cannot be seen but can be felt; some gases have a distinct smell; gases can flow or can be blown. On the basis of light passing through them, materials are classified as transparent (everything can be seen clearly), translucent (blurred outlines can be discerned and the color of things changes) and opaque (nothing can be seen through them).

Differentiate between melting and dissolving. Melting and dissolving are two different phenomena. Melting is the change of a solid into a liquid when it is heated, for example ice melts when it is taken out of the fridge or given heat; no other material is mixed with it. Dissolving takes place when a solid is mixed with a liquid: the solid disappears, spreads evenly through the liquid and is no longer visible, for example sugar or salt dissolving in water, or jelly crystals dissolving in hot water. The rate of dissolving depends on factors such as temperature (solids dissolve faster in hot water) and grain size (sugar powder dissolves faster in water than sugar grains).

What is a property? Describe the common properties of objects and materials. A property is a characteristic used to describe an object. Some properties describe the material the object is made of, such as color and texture, and some properties describe the object as a whole, such as shape and size. Common properties used to describe objects are color, shape, size, texture and weight. Children develop an operational understanding of property by identifying these common properties and recording them in a properties word bank. Weight is a property of an object which is a measure of how heavy or light an object is; it can be measured and compared using a pan balance and non-standard weights, and it depends on the size of the object and the material of which it is made. Students classify objects and materials on the basis of shared properties.

Describe the sequence of learning template and its phases. The sequence of learning template organizes a unit into phases. Phase A: Assessing prior knowledge, in which children's existing understanding is elicited, e.g. identifying common properties of materials and objects such as color, shape, pattern, size, texture and weight. Phase B: Developing a background, in which the topic is explored, e.g. exploring solids and liquids and developing the skill of classification. Phases C, D, E etc.: the main content of the unit/topic, e.g. changes such as dissolving and solidifying, making jelly, investigating physical changes and conducting fair tests. Final phase: Applying their skills and knowledge, in which students use what they have learnt in inquiry activities and are assessed. In the grade 2 unit on properties of solids and liquids, this template is broken down into ten lessons, each comprising two periods of 40 minutes.

What is classification? How do children learn to classify materials and liquids? Classification means grouping things or materials into classes using some property they share in common. Children learn classification by working with a variety of materials and liquids: they deepen and extend their observation skills to include classification, and they classify at different levels, from simple to complex. A simple step is matching liquids using a known property, or matching liquids using a secret property which others have to guess. A complex step is classifying the liquids into two and three groups using properties such as thick and thin, or transparent, translucent and opaque. Through collective discussion children share ideas, identify similarities and differences of a pair of liquids, and construct new understandings.

Explain the project research guideline for the research project on a manufactured object. In the research project, working in pairs, students select a manufactured object of common use (a bicycle is used as the case study) and research it over four weeks so that they make connections between the materials from which an object is made and the function of the object. The project research guideline has six steps: 1) Function of the object, an accurate description of what the object does or is used for. 2) Major materials, an accurate description of the major materials that make up the object. 3) Why these materials were chosen, including the properties of the materials which make them suitable for use in the object; the choice of material is a very important factor in project research. 4) Origin of one of the materials: (a) the raw materials from which the material is made, and (b) the processes the raw material undergoes to become the refined material used in the object. 5) History of the object: who invented it, when and where it first appeared, and how the original designs and choice of materials differ from those in use today. 6) A picture or photograph of the object.

State the do's and don'ts of evaluating students' work. Do's: acknowledge and encourage effort and progress, commenting on the specific work the student has done well; identify one or two important aspects for comment and review which are related to the planned learning goals; pinpoint weak aspects, such as misuse of a technical term, in a constructive way; give students time to read, reflect and respond to feedback, collectively or individually; and indicate the next steps clearly to the students. Don'ts: do not give judgmental comments, and above all scores or symbols (such as B+ or 8/10), especially while students are still constructing their concepts and skills, because these bring a closure to their efforts; do not pose rhetorical comments like "This needs improvement" or "This is below standards", as they do not inform the student about the nature of the work expected; and do not become too obsessive about the use of words or assertions students have made, since they are in the process of building their understanding and abilities.
